context: Legacy Berkeley DB wallet files are explicitly treated as adversarial input. Importing or migrating a crafted wallet reaches this parser before the records are trusted; a user must still select/load the wallet.
evidence: OverflowRecord supplies both the first page number and claimed item length. BerkeleyRODatabase::Open follows next_page until zero but neither records visited overflow pages nor requires each page to contribute data. OverflowPage accepts hf_offset == 0, so an OVERFLOW_DATA page whose next_page points to itself and whose hf_offset is zero leaves data.size() unchanged forever and never triggers the only size guard.
summary: A cyclic zero-length overflow-page chain makes the legacy Berkeley wallet parser loop indefinitely.

context: The parser is used for legacy Berkeley DB wallet migration and dump operations. Level checks prevent direct B-tree cycles, but do not prevent the same physical child page from being expanded repeatedly through duplicate references.
evidence: InternalRecord.page_num is wallet-controlled. The depth-first traversal pushes every nondeleted child reference and validates only that the referenced page has the expected level; it has no visited-page or work-budget check. A compact file can put many duplicate references to one next-level page at each level, causing that page and its descendants to be reparsed once per reference and multiplying work approximately by the branching factor at every level.
summary: Duplicate internal-page references can amplify parsing work exponentially for a small crafted Berkeley wallet.

context: A crafted encrypted wallet must be loaded and an authorized user or RPC client must attempt to unlock it. The expensive derivation runs while CWallet::Unlock holds cs_wallet, so the impact includes prolonged wallet unavailability rather than only a failed import.
evidence: CMasterKey serializes nDeriveIterations as an unsigned wallet-controlled value. LoadEncryptionKey deserializes and stores it without an upper bound. Unlock passes it to SetKeyFromPassphrase, which checks only rounds >= 1, implicitly converts it to the signed int count argument, and performs count-1 SHA-512 iterations. Values near INT_MAX cause billions of hashes; values above INT_MAX undergo implementation-defined conversion and can make the signed loop overflow without terminating normally.
summary: An unbounded wallet-controlled master-key iteration count can monopolize CPU during wallet unlock.
